lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.title: Guided practice B: informal comparative inference

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Read once, then cover the example and try the guided set from memory.

items.prompt: Sample A: 20, 22, 21, 23. Sample B: 15, 17, 16, 14. Based on the means, which sample tends to have greater values?

steps: Find the mean of Sample A: (20 + 22 + 21 + 23) ÷ 4 = 86 ÷ 4 = 21 1/2.
Find the mean of Sample B: (15 + 17 + 16 + 14) ÷ 4 = 62 ÷ 4 = 15 1/2.
Since 21 1/2 > 15 1/2, Sample A tends to have greater values.
workedSolution.answer: Sample A, with a mean of 21 1/2 compared to 15 1/2.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: Sample A: 33, 25, 31, 32, 30. Sample B: 15, 35, 25, 24, 15. Based on the range of each sample, which sample is more consistent (less variable)?
choices: Both samples have the same range.
Sample A, with a range of 8 compared to 20.
Sample B, with a range of 20 compared to 8.
Sample A, with a range of 20 compared to 8.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to know about all 440 shoppers at a grocery store. She randomly selects 102 of them to survey. What is the population in this situation?
choices: Only the first 102 shoppers at a grocery store on a list
The researcher's own estimate
The 102 randomly selected shoppers at a grocery store
All 440 shoppers at a grocery store

items.prompt: A student uses a random number generator to select 44 students at Lincoln Middle School from the full list, then surveys them. Is this sampling method likely to produce a representative sample?
choices: No, likely not representative — the method favors certain members over others.
Yes, likely representative, because the sample size is large enough.
Yes, likely representative — every member had a fair, known chance of being chosen.
No, likely not representative, because the population is too large.

items.prompt: In a random sample of 15 visitors to a science museum, 13 preferred a new park design. Based on this sample, about how many of the 120 visitors to a science museum would you expect to prefer a new park design?

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Five random samples of the same population produced these mean scores: 15, 9, 13, 15, 8. What is the range of these sample estimates?

A population has 2859 commuters on a train line. Student A takes a random sample of 6. Student B takes a random sample of 57. Both use proper random selection. Whose sample is more likely to give an estimate closer to the true population value?
choices: Student A's sample of 6, because smaller samples are easier to analyze.
Both are equally likely to be accurate, because both are random.
Student B's sample of 57, because larger random samples tend to produce more consistent, accurate estimates.
Neither sample is reliable unless it includes the entire population.

items.prompt: A student surveys 41 shoppers at a grocery store using a simple random sample and records the results. Is it valid to generalize this result to all 1435 shoppers at a grocery store?
choices: No, because samples can never be generalized to a population.
Yes, because the sample was selected randomly, so it is likely representative of the population.
Yes, because the sample size is large enough regardless of how it was chosen.
No, because the sample was not randomly selected, so it may not represent the population.

items.prompt: A sample of 7 values is: 65, 47, 50, 57, 47, 50, 56. What is the median of this data set?
